The Portobello Coade Stone Pillars
Three ornamental Coade stone pillars, (figure 1), form 
the focal point of the community garden on the 
Promenade at the foot of John Street, Portobello. The 
pillars, which date from the early 19th Century, used to 
stand in the garden of Argyle House, Hope Lane, off 
Portobello High Street, (figure 2). A map of 1890 shows 
the three pillars in the garden of the house, which was 
then the manse of St James’s Church, but it is not known 
how the pillars came to be in Portobello in the first place. 
In 1989, the City of Edinburgh Council granted planning 
permission for an extension to be built on to the front of 
the 1820s house, which was to be converted into flats, 
without making arrangements for the safekeeping of the 
pillars which were listed structures. 
Portobello Amenity Society members however turned up 
in force on the day the bulldozers toppled the pillars and 
succeeded in having the sections of the pillars rescued and 
placed in council storage, with the council accepting 
responsibility for and ownership of the pillars. Since then, 
Portobello Amenity Society campaigned to have the 
pillars re-erected on a suitable site in Portobello. 
Research by Celia Butterworth, a member of the society, 
proved that the pillars were Coade stone and that the 
designs on the two smaller pillars were identical to the 
Coade stone chimneys of Dalmeny House, built in 1817, 
near South Queensferry, seat of Lord Rosebery, (figure 3). 
There are three designs on the Dalmeny chimneys and on 
the two smaller Portobello pillars - the fleur-de-lis, Tudor 
rose and crown and lion. The rose refers to the Rosebery 
name and it’s possible that the flower held by the lion 
may be a primrose, (figure 4), Primrose being the family 
name of the Earl of Rosebery. Records show that around 
1820, £3,800 worth of Coade stone, which included 
decorations in addition to the chimneys, was shipped to 
Leith from the Coade factory in Lambeth so it is possible 
that some of the chimney sections came to Portobello 
then. The third larger Coade stone pillar which stood in 
the garden of Argyle House has a hoop and fleur-de-lis 
design, quite different from the “Dalmeny” designs. Its 
construction is also different as it is made up of 
complete circles whereas the circles of the two smaller 
pillars are made up of quadrants. The larger pillar was 
not designed as a chimney and its origin is unknown.
By 2005 the City of Edinburgh Council had agreed that 
the pillars could be re-erected in a new community garden 
to be built to replace a disused paddling pool on 
Portobello Promenade and that they would maintain the 
pillars. As the council was unable to fund the restoration 
and re-erection of the pillars, Portobello Amenity Society 
made an application to the Heritage Lottery Fund, which 
was successful, and was granted £49,700 which was about 
80% of the total cost. The council contributed by building 
foundations for the pillars and providing the internal 
metal supports for each pillar, while Portobello 
Community Council and Portobello Amenity Society each 
contributed £2,400. 
Since the pillars’ removal from the garden of Argyle 
House, the council had stored them in various locations, 
often in jumbled piles outdoors. One location was next to 
a recycling depot, (figure 5), which resulted in eight of the 
quadrants decorated with the lion holding the primrose 
being stolen. Several of the quadrants had been damaged 
when the pillars had been toppled and the various moves 
while in council storage had caused further damage.
As the pillars were to be re-erected as the centrepiece of a 
garden which was open to the public, it was necessary 
that each of the pillars should be supported by a designed 
internal metal rod which had metal brackets across its 
diameter, (figure 6). These held the rod tightly within the 
inner surface of the Coade quadrants of the two smaller 
pillars to provide the necessary rigidity. The same 
principle was used with the larger pillar which consisted 
of complete circles of a different design. The metal rod 
was screwed into the foundation of each pillar and into a 
metal cap at the top of the pillar thus ensuring the 
structural stability of each pillar. 
The pillars were expertly restored by Graciela Ainsworth 
and her team of sculpture conservators who removed 
several layers of paint of different colours from the 
pillars, the top layer being battleship grey, (figure 2), and 
repaired damaged sections. There were sufficient 
quadrants with the fleur-de-lis design to construct one 
pillar to match one of the Dalmeny chimneys. There was 
only one original base and crown top however so it made 
sense that one pillar should consist of original elements, 
(figure 7). The conservators made replacement quadrants, 
using a modern Coade mix, for the ones with the lion 
design that had been stolen. There were several blank 
quadrants in the pillars in the Argyle House garden which 
were placed between complete circles of the lion and the 
Tudor rose and crown designs to form the second smaller 
pillar.
As only one pillar had a crown top, it was decided that the 
other smaller pillar should have a matching new top. A 
local potter and amenity society member, Alison 
Robinson, after considerable trial and error, managed to 
recreate Mrs. Coade’s original Coade stone mix. She then 
made a new capital for the other smaller pillar. The 
sections of the capital were joined together with butterfly 
fixings which Alison also made, (figure 8), together with 
two quadrants with the Tudor rose and crown design to 
complete a circle.
 At the start of the project, it was planned to erect railings 
round the pillars as a form of protection. However, it was 
finally decided that railings might prove problematic and 
might actually encourage youngsters to climb over them 
to access the pillars. The planting of prickly plants, such 
as berberis, round and between the pillars was decided on 
instead. When this was decided, the three pillars had been 
erected, the two smaller ones with tops, the larger one as 
it had been in its original location, without a top. The 
general feeling of those on the committee organising the 
project was that it looked rather odd having one pillar 
without a top.
Alison bravely decided to make a new top for the 
remaining pillar in her own Coade stone mix as the 
money which had been set aside for the railings could now 
be used for this purpose. While the making of a smaller 
capital had not been without its problems, the huge size 
and scale of the larger top presented Alison with 
enormous difficulties. Viewed from the ground, the top 
she created looks far smaller than it actually is. It consists 
of 24 sections, each section being of a very complex shape. 
In actuality the finished top measures five feet in width 
and two feet in depth. Twelve of the largest sections, 
which Alison had made in her workshop, could not fit into 
her own kiln and had to be fired at Ibstock Scottish Brick 
in Glasgow, where half of the pieces exploded after 
leaving the kiln, possibly due to residual moisture, and 
had to be made again. Alison overcame all of these 
difficulties and the larger pillar now with its new top 
looks splendid.  
For our application to the Heritage Lottery Fund to be 
successful, the society had to prove that there was a huge 
amount of support from the community for the project. 
This we did in several ways. Meetings were held to inform 
the public about the intended project. A window display 
was set up in Portobello library which included several of 
the pillar quadrants, explaining how they would be 
cleaned. Alison organised several very well attended events 
for local children in the community centre and the local 
primary school at which model pillars were built out of 
carpet tubes with prizes being given for the best decorated 
pillars, (figure 9). She also held several tile making 
sessions at which children press moulded tiles in modern 
Coade with either their name or handprint. The tiles were 
later taken away to be fired and then returned to the 
children. A public talk was also held, on ‘Edinburgh 
Monuments’ which included the pillars. Once the pillars 
had been erected, another public talk was held at which 
Celia talked about the history of the pillars, Alison about 
making the smaller new capital, while Graciella explained 
how the pillars were cleaned, restored and erected.
Today the pillars are much loved by local residents and 
much admired by visitors. The project not only preserved 
part of Portobello’s history but provides an attractive 
focus to the community garden on the promenade. It is 
also a testament to the determination and talent of local 
people who wanted to preserve part of Portobello’s past 
and to the skill of the conservators who repaired and re-
erected the pillars.
John Stewart, Chair, Portobello Amenity Society,                            
                       Director, Portobello Heritage Trust
